faq.q: Why is a temporal bone fracture dangerous?

faq.a: Weber and Rinne tuning‑fork tests; Weber lateralises to the better‑conducting ear, Rinne compares bone vs. air conduction.
faq.q: What bedside test helps differentiate conductive from sensorineural loss?

faq.a: Through the thin bone to the posterior cranial fossa or sigmoid sinus, potentially causing meningitis or venous sinus thrombosis.

exam: A patient with a road‑traffic accident presents with hemotympanum and battle’s sign — what is your next immediate investigation and why? — CT head to rule out epidural hematoma; early detection saves life.

How would you differentiate a longitudinal from a transverse temporal bone fracture on imaging? — Longitudinal follows the squamous part, often spares the inner ear; transverse crosses the petrous part, more likely to injure facial/vestibulocochlear nerves.

A child develops facial palsy 48 h after a head injury; what is the most likely site of nerve injury and management? — Likely facial canal within the petrous bone; start steroids, monitor, consider EMG if no improvement.

Explain why a patient with a temporal bone fracture may develop CSF otorrhea and the steps to manage it in a low‑resource setting. — Fracture tears the dura over the middle ear; place head elevation, avoid Valsalva, give prophylactic antibiotics, arrange surgical repair if leak persists.
What are the key features on bedside examination that suggest a basilar skull fracture? — Battle’s sign, raccoon eyes, CSF otorrhea/rhinorrhea, hemotympanum, cranial nerve deficits.

In a malaria‑endemic region, a patient with fever and new hearing loss is found to have a temporal bone osteomyelitis — what organisms are likely and initial therapy? — Pseudomonas aeruginosa (common), consider Staphylococcus aureus; start broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics covering gram‑negatives, adjust when cultures return.
Why is a plain skull X‑ray insufficient for diagnosing a transverse temporal bone fracture? — It may miss petrous involvement; CT provides detailed bone windows needed for surgical planning.

During a head‑injury assessment, you note a patient’s ear drum is bulging and blood‑filled — what does this indicate and what should you do? — Hemotympanum suggests middle ear bleed; assess for temporal bone fracture and obtain CT; monitor for epidural bleed.
ai.title: Temporal Bone Anatomy
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The temporal bone houses the structures of hearing and balance and forms the lateral skull base. Understanding its relations, blood and nerve supply is essential for diagnosing fractures, infections and skull-base tumors, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Divided into squamous (flat), tympanic (surrounds external auditory canal), mastoid (air cells), petrous (dense, houses inner ear).
Key for protecting the inner ear, facial nerve, and major vessels.
sections.p: The temporal bone is a complex, pyramidal bone forming the lateral wall of the skull and the floor of the middle and posterior cranial fossae. It consists of four parts: squamous, tympanic, mastoid and petrous.

b: External auditory canal runs in the tympanic part.
Mastoid process contains air cells communicating with the middle ear.
Petrous apex contacts the sphenoid bone.
sections.p: It lies inferior to the temporal lobe, posterior to the zygomatic arch and superior to the neck of the mandible. The petrous portion projects medially and contains the internal acoustic meatus.

b: Facial nerve (VII) passes through the facial canal in the petrous part.
Middle meningeal artery runs in the groove on the inner surface of the squamous part.
sections.p: Anteriorly it contacts the sphenoid; posteriorly the occipital bone; medially the parietal bone; inferiorly the mandible and styloid process of the temporal bone.

b: Middle meningeal artery is most commonly injured in temporal bone fractures.
Petrosal veins drain the inner ear and communicate with the cavernous sinus.
sections.p: Arterial supply comes from branches of the external carotid (posterior auricular, occipital, middle meningeal) and internal carotid (internal auditory artery). Venous drainage follows the emissary veins to the sigmoid sinus.

b: Facial nerve palsy suggests petrous fracture.
Loss of hearing/vertigo indicates VIII nerve involvement.
sections.p: Sensory innervation is via the auriculotemporal branch of V3 and the great auricular nerve (C2‑C3). The facial nerve traverses the bone, and the vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII) exits via the internal acoustic meatus.

b: Mastoid air cells help equalise middle‑ear pressure.
Petrous part shields the inner ear and vestibular system.
sections.p: Provides attachment for muscles of mastication, supports the auditory apparatus, and protects the brainstem and cranial nerves VII and VIII.

b: Fracture types: longitudinal (middle meningeal artery injury) vs. transverse (facial nerve, inner ear damage).
Complications: epidural hematoma, CSF otorrhea, facial palsy, hearing loss, mastoiditis.
sections.p: Temporal bone fractures are common in road‑traffic accidents and falls. In low‑resource settings, delayed presentation and limited imaging increase morbidity.

t.b: Detects fracture line, hematoma, and middle ear involvement; if unavailable, plain skull X‑ray can suggest a longitudinal fracture.
Assesses conductive vs. sensorineural loss; if not available, bedside tuning‑fork tests (Weber, Rinne) guide management.
Evaluates severity of palsy; if unavailable, clinical House‑Brackmann grading is used.

b: Battle’s sign appears 1‑3 days after fracture; indicates basilar skull injury.
Hemotympanum suggests middle ear bleed; may accompany middle meningeal artery injury.
sections.p: At the bedside, look for battle’s sign (mastoid ecchymosis), raccoon eyes (periorbital ecchymosis), CSF otorrhea, hemotympanum, and facial weakness.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening headache or vomiting (possible epidural hematoma).
New facial paralysis or loss of hearing after head trauma.
Clear fluid leaking from ear or nose (CSF leak).
